practice_questions.text: Which term describes the process by which producers filter events through their own values and perspectives before presenting them to audiences?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Mediation (C). Distractors: A) Encoding; B) Anchorage; D) Verisimilitude.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which a magazine producer uses selection when putting together a front cover.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Award for any valid act of selection, e.g. choice of cover image; choice of cover lines; decision to use a celebrity image rather than news content; choice of which stories to highlight.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why a media product can never be a completely neutral or transparent record of reality.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct reasons, e.g. producers must select what to include and exclude; the medium itself shapes meaning; construction choices (framing, editing, music) add meaning; mediation introduces the values and perspectives of producers; commercial or institutional pressures influence what is shown.

practice_questions.text: Explain what Marshall McLuhan meant by the idea that "the medium is the message", using an example from a media form you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation that the medium's form and properties shape meaning regardless of content, with a specific, well-developed example that illustrates how different media forms produce different meanings from the same event or story.
Secure: Accurate explanation of the idea with a relevant example that is briefly developed.
Developing: Some understanding of the idea, perhaps expressed vaguely; example may be present but undeveloped or only partially relevant.
Emerging: Limited or confused understanding; example absent or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the processes of selection, construction and mediation work together to shape the meaning of a news broadcast you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three processes named and accurately defined, each illustrated with a specific detail from a studied product; explanation shows how the three processes interlock to produce a coherent preferred reading.
Secure: All three processes addressed and mostly accurate; at least one is illustrated with a specific example; interplay between processes noted.
Developing: Two of the three processes addressed with some accuracy; example present but one-sided; limited sense of how the processes interlock.
Emerging: One process addressed or all three named without accurate definition; little or no specific example.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the concept of re-presentation can be applied to a media product you have studied. In your answer, consider how selection, construction and mediation shape the version of reality the product creates, and evaluate the view that it is impossible for any media product to be truly objective.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, well-structured argument with a clear thesis about re-presentation; all three processes identified and applied to specific moments in a named product with perceptive analysis; theoretical framework used accurately throughout; counter-position or complication considered; coherent conclusion.
Secure: Clear argument addressing re-presentation across the product; selection, construction and mediation all present; examples from the product anchor the analysis; mostly accurate use of framework terminology; some evaluative thinking.
Developing: Some understanding of re-presentation; at least two processes addressed; examples present but analysis may be descriptive; limited evaluation of the objectivity question.
Emerging: Basic points about media not being neutral; limited or inaccurate use of terminology; answer is mainly descriptive with little framework analysis.

practice_questions.text: Which term describes a company that owns businesses at multiple stages of the same media supply chain, such as production, distribution and exhibition?
practice_questions.marks: Vertical integration. Distractor check: horizontal integration = same level, not multiple stages; diversification = different sectors; synergy = mutual promotion.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way a media conglomerate might use synergy to profit from a single media product.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any valid example: licensing merchandise, releasing a video game tie-in, launching a streaming spin-off series, opening a theme-park attraction, cross-promoting on conglomerate-owned channels.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain one difference between vertical integration and horizontal integration.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for correctly identifying the difference (vertical = different stages of supply chain; horizontal = same stage/level). One mark for a clear explanation anchored to the direction of expansion, e.g. vertical integration means owning production and distribution whereas horizontal means owning multiple studios.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'concentration of ownership' in the media industries and why some critics argue it is a concern.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear, developed explanation of concentration of ownership; specific reference to how fewer owners controlling more content can limit the diversity of voices and perspectives available to audiences; analytical engagement with why this matters beyond commercial efficiency.
Secure: Accurate explanation of concentration; some engagement with its consequences for diversity or public debate.
Developing: Basic explanation of what concentration means; limited analysis of why it is considered a problem.
Emerging: Vague or partial definition; consequences not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a global media conglomerate might use diversification to reduce commercial risk, using an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of diversification as expanding into different sectors to spread financial risk; detailed and specific worked example showing how revenue from one division offsets losses in another; clear link between the strategy and its commercial purpose.
Secure: Clear explanation of diversification; relevant example that illustrates the concept; link to risk reduction made.
Developing: Some explanation of diversification; example is present but underdeveloped or only loosely linked.
Emerging: Basic or confused definition; example missing or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Using the ideas of Curran and Seaton, analyse how patterns of ownership in the media industry affect the range of content and voices available to audiences.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, accurate application of Curran and Seaton's argument about power and concentrated ownership; detailed analysis of how ownership patterns shape content diversity; specific and relevant industry examples used analytically, not descriptively; counter-position acknowledged (e.g. independent sector or market-diversity argument).
Secure: Accurate reference to Curran and Seaton; clear argument about ownership and content diversity; relevant examples; some analytical depth.
Developing: Curran and Seaton named but theory not fully applied; argument about ownership and content present but limited; examples may be vague.
Emerging: Curran and Seaton mentioned in passing or misattributed; mainly descriptive account of who owns what; limited analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the term 'anchorage' in media language analysis?
A. The way an image is composed within a frame
B. The use of text to fix the preferred meaning of an image
C. A sign that physically resembles what it represents
D. The literal, factual level of meaning in a media product
practice_questions.marks: B — The use of text to fix the preferred meaning of an image. Do not accept A (composition), C (iconic sign) or D (denotation).

practice_questions.text: Identify one example of a symbolic sign in a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for any clearly described symbolic sign with a named media product. Example: a crown worn by a character in a drama series symbolises authority or royalty. The connection must be culturally agreed rather than physically motivated.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way a media producer uses direct address and explain the effect it creates.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a clear example of direct address in a named media product (e.g. a magazine cover where the subject looks directly into the camera). 1 further mark for explaining the effect — e.g. it creates a personal connection with the viewer or invites the audience into a relationship with the subject.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Roland Barthes's concept of connotation can help analyse a media product.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: defines connotation as meaning beyond the literal (1 mark). Developing: applies connotation to a specific element in a named media product (2 marks). Secure/Mastering: explains how connotative meaning depends on cultural context and gives a detailed example from a media product you have studied (3 marks). No marks for pure theory recall without application.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a media producer uses signs and codes to communicate a particular message to their audience. Refer to a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: basic description of a sign or code, limited application (1 mark). Developing: names a relevant sign or code and attempts to link it to meaning (2 marks). Secure: identifies specific signs/codes and explains clearly how they create meaning for the audience in a named product (3 marks). Mastering: analyses how the choice of signs and codes works together to construct a particular message, with precise terminology (denotation, connotation, anchorage, code type) and a clear link to the intended audience effect (4 marks).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the concept of semiotics, including denotation, connotation and anchorage, can be applied to the way meaning is communicated in a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging (1-2): simple identification of one or two surface-level features; limited or no use of semiotic terminology.
Developing (3-4): explains denotation and/or connotation with reference to the named product; some accurate use of terminology but analysis may be inconsistent or underdeveloped.
Secure (5): clear and accurate analysis using at least two semiotic concepts (e.g. denotation/connotation plus anchorage or code); well-chosen examples from the product.
Mastering (6): sophisticated and sustained analysis integrating multiple semiotic concepts; explains how the combination of signs, codes and anchorage constructs a specific meaning for a defined audience; precise and fluent use of media language terminology throughout.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following best describes the hypodermic needle model of media effects?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct answer is C. A) Incorrect — this describes Uses and Gratifications. B) Incorrect — this describes the two-step flow. C) Correct — the hypodermic model proposes direct, immediate and uniform effects on a passive audience. D) Incorrect — this describes cultivation theory.

practice_questions.text: Identify the researcher whose Bobo doll experiment (1961) provided experimental support for the idea that audiences can learn behaviour from media.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Albert Bandura. Award mark for full name; do not award for 'Bandura' alone without context making it clear the student means Albert Bandura.

practice_questions.text: Identify the two-step flow model and explain one way it challenged the passive audience model.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying that messages pass through opinion leaders before reaching the wider audience. 1 mark for a developed point explaining that this means the audience is not uniformly and directly affected (e.g. social relationships and conversations filter the message; not everyone receives the same effect).

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the term 'personal identity' as a need in Blumler and Katz's Uses and Gratifications theory.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Names the personal identity need and gives a vague definition. Secure: Accurately defines personal identity as the need to find values, attitudes or lifestyle choices reflected in media. Mastering: Accurate definition plus a specific, well-developed example (e.g. a viewer choosing media content that reinforces their political outlook, cultural background or self-image) with a clear explanation of how this demonstrates the theory.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Gerbner's cultivation theory and Mean World Syndrome suggest that media exposure can affect audiences over time.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Shows awareness that heavy media use changes how people see the world, but explanation is vague. Secure: Correctly describes cultivation theory as the gradual shaping of worldview through heavy viewing and identifies Mean World Syndrome as the distorted belief that the world is more violent than it is. Mastering: Full, precise explanation of both concepts with a clear account of how heavy television viewing cultivates an exaggerated sense of danger, linked to the broader media effects debate and the contrast with active audience models.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Blumler and Katz's Uses and Gratifications theory can be applied to explain how audiences use a media form you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Mentions one or two needs with limited or no connection to a specific product. Developing: Applies two or three needs to a named media form but the analysis is surface-level; the link between the theory and the product's features is not clearly explained. Secure: Applies at least three of the four needs accurately to a specific media form, with clear explanation of how features of the product satisfy each need. Mastering: Sustained analytical argument across all four needs, with precise reference to specific elements of a named media form; acknowledges at least one limitation of the theory (e.g. unconscious habit use, or the theory ignores industry power) and links to the broader active/passive debate.

practice_questions.text: Which theorist is associated with the concept of the male gaze?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: B) Laura Mulvey. Distractors: A) Stuart Hall; C) Judith Butler; D) bell hooks.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which a music video might display the male gaze through camera choices.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Award for any valid camera choice, e.g. slow pan across a female performer's body; close-up fragmenting a female performer; low-angle shot emphasising physical appearance; lingering shot on a female figure while male figures are shown in action.

practice_questions.text: Give two differences between an essentialist and a social constructionist view of gender.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct differences: essentialism sees gender as natural/biological vs social constructionism sees it as culturally constructed; essentialism implies representations reflect reality vs social constructionism implies they create and reinforce norms; essentialism suggests gender is fixed vs social constructionism allows for gender to change over time.

practice_questions.text: Explain how stereotypes enable audiences to interpret a media product quickly, and why this is also a limitation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation of the cognitive shortcut function with a specific example; equally clear explanation of at least one limitation (e.g. reduction of individuality, reinforcement of power imbalances, naturalisation of prejudice), well developed.
Secure: Accurate explanation of both the use and the limitation, with at least a brief example.
Developing: One side more developed than the other; explanation present but may be general.
Emerging: Basic identification of stereotype as oversimplification; limited development of use or limitation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Mulvey's concept of the male gaze can be applied to representations of women in advertising you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate account of Mulvey's theory with all three gazes identified; specific advertising example with detailed analysis of how each gaze operates within the product; sustained connection between camera choices and the positioning of women as spectacle.
Secure: Accurate account of the male gaze; at least one specific advertising example; two of the three gazes present; analysis mostly developed.
Developing: Mulvey's theory summarised but not fully developed; one example present; analysis may be descriptive; one or two gazes mentioned.
Emerging: Basic reference to women being shown as objects; Mulvey's name may be mentioned but theory is inaccurate or absent; little specific example.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how gender representation in a media product you have studied reflects either an essentialist or a social constructionist view of gender. In your answer, consider the role of stereotyping and evaluate whether the representation challenges or reinforces dominant ideas about gender.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear thesis on essentialism or social constructionism; both concepts accurately defined and applied to specific moments in a named product; stereotyping discussed with nuance (uses and problems); evaluation of whether the product challenges or reinforces norms, with counter-position considered; Mulvey or another theorist used accurately to support the argument; coherent structure throughout.
Secure: Clear argument with essentialism and social constructionism both present; stereotyping addressed; examples from the product anchor the analysis; mostly accurate use of theory; some evaluative thinking.
Developing: One of the two theoretical positions addressed in more depth; stereotyping present; examples used but analysis may be descriptive; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Basic identification of stereotypes in a product; limited or no accurate use of essentialism or social constructionism; answer is mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is an example of guerrilla marketing?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct answer is B. A) Incorrect — this is paid media advertising. B) Correct — an unannounced installation in a public space to generate surprise and conversation is guerrilla marketing. C) Incorrect — this is a traditional trailer. D) Incorrect — this is owned media.

practice_questions.text: Identify the term for the additional audience a media product may reach beyond its primary target group.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: secondary audience.

practice_questions.text: Identify what an 'audience profile' is and explain one reason why media organisations construct them.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for defining audience profile as a constructed set of assumptions about the typical target audience member. 1 mark for a developed reason — for example, to ensure every creative and marketing decision is directed at the most likely consumers, or to demonstrate to advertisers that the product reaches a specific, valuable group.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'viral marketing' and why media organisations use it.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Gives a basic definition of viral marketing as something that spreads online. Secure: Accurately defines viral marketing as a strategy designed to encourage audiences to share content voluntarily and explains that it generates earned media reach without proportional advertising spend. Mastering: Precise definition plus a well-developed explanation of why this is commercially valuable (credibility of organic sharing, cost efficiency, audience-as-distributor logic), with a clear example context.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of a teaser campaign reflects the assumptions a media organisation makes about its target audience.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Notes that teasers withhold information but does not connect this to audience assumptions. Secure: Explains that teaser campaigns are designed to generate curiosity and conversation, and that this reflects an assumption that the target audience is engaged enough to seek out further information and discuss the product socially. Mastering: Full explanation linking specific teaser design choices (withholding plot, focusing on tone) to detailed audience assumptions (the audience is digitally active, genre-literate, and values anticipation) and connecting to the concept of earned media.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a media organisation uses different marketing techniques to reach a target audience for a product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names one or two marketing techniques with limited connection to audience assumptions. Developing: Identifies two or three techniques with some explanation of how each targets the audience, but the analysis lacks depth; connections to audience profiling are superficial. Secure: Analyses at least three techniques with clear explanation of how each reflects assumptions about the target audience; uses appropriate terminology (primary audience, earned media, viral, niche/mass). Mastering: Sustained analytical argument comparing the effectiveness of different techniques, with precise reference to a named product's marketing strategy; explicitly links marketing choices to audience profile assumptions and connects to broader industry context (paid/owned/earned framework).

before.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to explain targeting or marketing techniques, name the specific technique, explain how it works, and then link it to the assumptions the producer is making about their target audience. The examiner wants to see that you understand the relationship between audience profiling and the marketing choices made — not just a description of what a trailer is.

practice_questions.text: Which phase of media production involves editing, colour grading and mixing the soundtrack?
practice_questions.marks: Post-production. Distractor check: pre-production = planning; production = filming/recording; commissioning = pre-production sub-phase.

practice_questions.text: Identify one role that is typically completed during the pre-production phase of a television drama.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any valid pre-production role: writing or developing the script, casting performers, scouting locations, drawing up a production schedule, agreeing a budget, commissioning.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain how outsourcing affects the working practices of a large media organisation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying outsourcing (contracting external companies or freelancers to complete specific work). One mark for a clear explanation of its effect, e.g. it reduces the organisation's permanent workforce costs and allows flexibility, but means many workers are on short-term contracts rather than permanent employment.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'streaming-first commissioning' and how it differs from traditional broadcast working practices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of streaming-first commissioning; clear contrast with broadcast working practices in terms of release strategy, audience measurement and production economics; analytical engagement with how the commissioning platform shapes the product.
Secure: Accurate explanation of streaming-first; some contrast with broadcast drawn; limited analytical depth.
Developing: Basic explanation of what streaming-first means; contrast with broadcast vague or incomplete.
Emerging: Vague response; streaming and broadcast differences not clearly explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of freelance and outsourced labour shapes the working practices of the media industries, with reference to a specific media form.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of freelance and outsourced working practices; well-chosen, specific example from a named media form; clear link between working practice and its commercial or creative consequences for the organisation and/or the workers.
Secure: Clear explanation of outsourcing/freelance; relevant example; link to consequences made.
Developing: Some explanation; example present but underdeveloped or weakly linked.
Emerging: Basic or confused account; example missing or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how decisions made during pre-production and post-production shape the final form and meaning of a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis connecting specific pre-production decisions (budget, casting, scripting) and post-production choices (editing rhythm, colour grade, sound design) to observable qualities in a named Close Study Product; argument about how production conditions determine meaning, not just content; relevant theoretical framing (e.g. industries framework).
Secure: Clear analysis of pre-production and post-production decisions; reference to a studied product; some connection between decisions and the finished product's qualities.
Developing: Some engagement with production phases; product referenced but analysis is mainly descriptive.
Emerging: Basic or confused account of production phases; mainly narrative or descriptive; reference to product minimal.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the term 'mediation' in media studies?
A. The process of fixing the preferred meaning of an image using text
B. The process by which events are filtered and shaped by media producers before reaching audiences
C. The level of formality in a media text's language and tone
D. The way an image is composed within the camera frame
practice_questions.marks: B — The process by which events are filtered and shaped by media producers before reaching audiences. Do not accept A (anchorage), C (register) or D (composition/framing in the physical sense).

practice_questions.text: Identify one way a media producer uses exclusion to shape the meaning of a media product.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for a clearly stated example of exclusion (e.g. a news broadcast that does not include the perspective of a particular group, or a documentary that edits out contradictory evidence). The student must indicate what is excluded and how that shapes meaning.

practice_questions.text: Identify one technique a media producer uses to create verisimilitude and explain the effect it has.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a specific technique used to create the impression of reality (e.g. handheld camera movement, naturalistic lighting, improvised-sounding dialogue). 1 further mark for explaining why this technique makes the product feel authentic or realistic to the audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 'preferred meaning' and why it matters for media analysis.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: defines preferred meaning as the intended message of the producer (1 mark). Developing: explains that producers encode preferred meanings through selection and combination of signs (2 marks). Secure/Mastering: adds that audiences may not always accept the preferred meaning, and links this to the constructed nature of media reality (3 marks).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a media producer uses framing and selection to construct a particular point of view. Refer to a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: limited description of framing or selection without clear application (1 mark). Developing: identifies one example of framing or selection and attempts to link it to meaning (2 marks). Secure: clearly explains how framing and/or selection choices in a named product construct a specific viewpoint, with accurate use of terminology (3 marks). Mastering: analyses how framing and selection work together to construct a sustained point of view, with reference to specific moments in the named product and explanation of what has been excluded or marginalised (4 marks).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the processes of selection, combination and exclusion are used in a media product you have studied to construct a version of reality that reflects the values of the producer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging (1-2): identifies one or two surface-level choices in the product; limited engagement with the idea of construction.
Developing (3-4): explains how selection and/or combination choices shape meaning; some reference to the named product; may not address exclusion or producer values.
Secure (5): clear and sustained analysis of how selection, combination and exclusion work together in the named product to construct a particular version of reality; engages with whose values or viewpoint is reflected.
Mastering (6): sophisticated analysis integrating all three processes (selection, combination, exclusion) with precise terminology; argues convincingly that the product encodes a specific ideological or commercial viewpoint and links this to the techniques used; well-chosen, specific references throughout.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes NRS social grade A?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct answer is C. A) Incorrect — D describes semi-skilled and unskilled manual workers; E includes state pensioners, casual and lowest-grade workers, and people unemployed with state benefits only. B) Incorrect — C2 describes skilled manual workers. C) Correct — grade A is higher managerial, administrative or professional. D) Incorrect — this describes grade B.

practice_questions.text: Identify the organisation responsible for measuring television viewing figures in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: BARB (Broadcasters' Audience Research Board). Award mark for either the abbreviation or the full name.

practice_questions.text: Identify psychographic segmentation and explain one advantage it has over demographic segmentation for media producers.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for defining psychographic segmentation as dividing audiences by attitudes, values, interests and lifestyles. 1 mark for a developed advantage — for example, it allows targeting based on motivation and identity rather than just measurable social characteristics, meaning marketing can speak directly to why a person might want the product.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between 'reach' and 'share' as audience measurement terms.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Gives a basic distinction between the two terms without precise definitions. Secure: Accurately defines reach as the number or percentage of people who view a specified minimum amount of a broadcast and share as the percentage of the television audience watching a particular channel at a given time. Mastering: Accurate definitions plus a developed explanation of how each figure is used differently by the industry — for example, share reveals competitive performance against other channels at the same time, while reach is more important for demonstrating total audience size to advertisers.

practice_questions.text: Explain how BARB collects audience data and why this data is important to commercial television broadcasters.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Shows basic awareness that BARB measures viewing but explanation is limited or inaccurate. Secure: Correctly explains that BARB uses a representative household panel with electronic meters, collecting daily viewing data; explains that this informs advertising rates and commissioning decisions. Mastering: Full, accurate explanation of the BARB methodology plus a clear account of two or more ways the data is used commercially (advertising rates, scheduling, programme commissioning) with a precise explanation of why the representativeness of the panel is important for credibility.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the different methods of audience categorisation help a media organisation to target and sell advertising to a specific audience.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names one or two segmentation methods with limited explanation. Developing: Describes two methods with some explanation of how they are used, but links to advertising are vague. Secure: Explains demographic, psychographic and/or geographic segmentation clearly and shows how each type of data serves a different purpose for advertisers; references a named audience research body. Mastering: Sustained analytical argument explaining how the three segmentation types work together — for example, how NRS grades define the demographic target, psychographic profiling refines why they would respond to the product, and geographic data determines where to run the campaign; connects to the commercial logic of advertising rates and audience measurement.

practice_questions.text: Which theorist argued that convergence is a cultural shift as well as a technological one, describing it as a world in which old and new media collide?
practice_questions.marks: Henry Jenkins. Distractor check: Stuart Hall = encoding/decoding, representation theory; Curran and Seaton = ownership and power; David Hesmondhalgh = cultural industries.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which convergence has changed the way audiences engage with media products.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any valid example: second-screen viewing, engaging with transmedia storytelling across platforms, discussing content on social media while watching, accessing the same content across multiple devices.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain what is meant by 'transmedia storytelling'.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying transmedia storytelling (a story that unfolds across multiple platforms). One mark for explaining how it works, e.g. each platform (film, game, social media, comic) adds something unique to the narrative, so the audience must engage across several forms to experience the full story.

practice_questions.text: Explain what cross-media ownership means and why it gives a conglomerate significant power in the media landscape.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition of cross-media ownership; clear and developed analysis of the power it generates through control of content, distribution network and platform simultaneously; reference to data collection or terms-of-access leverage.
Secure: Accurate definition; some explanation of the power advantage; limited analytical depth.
Developing: Basic definition; power advantage acknowledged but not well explained.
Emerging: Vague or partial definition; reasons for power advantage missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the convergence of content, network and platform providers has changed the media landscape, using an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation of how convergence brings together previously separate industry roles; specific and well-developed example showing all three provider types integrated in one organisation; analytical link between convergence and consequences for audiences or competitors.
Secure: Accurate explanation of convergence; relevant example; link to consequences made.
Developing: Some explanation; example present but underdeveloped or weakly integrated.
Emerging: Basic or confused account of convergence; example missing or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Using Henry Jenkins' ideas about convergence culture, analyse how a media product you have studied uses multiple platforms to engage its audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, accurate application of Jenkins' convergence theory, distinguishing technological and cultural dimensions; detailed analysis of how a specific studied product extends across platforms; specific examples of how each platform contributes differently to the audience experience; acknowledgement of the limits or counter-arguments to Jenkins' optimistic view of active audiences.
Secure: Accurate reference to Jenkins; clear argument about cross-platform engagement; relevant product examples; some analytical depth.
Developing: Jenkins named but theory not fully applied; product referenced but mainly descriptive; cross-platform argument limited.
Emerging: Jenkins mentioned vaguely or misattributed; mainly descriptive; product examples absent or underdeveloped.

before.exam_tip_html: When applying Jenkins’ convergence theory in an extended response, do not simply say “convergence means everything is on one device.” The strongest answers distinguish between technological convergence (devices and platforms merging) and cultural convergence (audiences engaging across platforms as active participants), then show how a specific media product or industry illustrates both dimensions. Examiners reward the distinction between the two levels of convergence.

practice_questions.text:
In Propp's theory, which character function describes the figure who sends the hero on the quest?
A. Helper
B. Donor
C. Dispatcher
D. False hero
practice_questions.marks: C — Dispatcher. Do not accept A (helper supports the hero but does not initiate the quest), B (donor provides a gift or skill), or D (false hero appears heroic but is not).

practice_questions.text: Identify the stage in Todorov's narrative arc that immediately follows the disruption.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for 'recognition' (the characters acknowledge that something has gone wrong). Do not accept 'repair' (this is the stage after recognition) or 'new equilibrium'.

practice_questions.text: Identify one example of the enigma code in a media product you have studied and explain how it engages the audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for clearly identifying a specific unresolved question or puzzle in a named media product. 1 further mark for explaining how this enigma creates suspense or compels the audience to continue watching, reading or playing.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Todorov's narrative theory can be used to analyse the structure of a media product.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: names Todorov and/or describes one stage of the arc (1 mark). Developing: accurately describes the five-stage arc and attempts to apply it to a named product (2 marks). Secure/Mastering: clearly applies at least three stages of the arc to specific moments in a named product and explains how the structure shapes the audience's engagement (3 marks).

practice_questions.text: Explain how Propp's character functions can be used to analyse a media product you have studied, and what this analysis reveals about the values encoded in that product.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: identifies one or two character functions with limited application (1 mark). Developing: maps two or three functions onto characters in a named product (2 marks). Secure: accurately maps multiple functions and begins to comment on what the distribution of active and passive roles reveals about the product's values (3 marks). Mastering: sophisticated application of Propp's functions to a named product, with analysis of which character types dominate, which are absent or subverted, and what this encodes about gender, power or ideology (4 marks).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how narrative theory (including at least one named theorist) can be applied to a media product you have studied to explain how it engages its audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging (1-2): brief description of narrative structure or named theorist with little or no application to a specific product.
Developing (3-4): applies one theoretical framework (Propp or Todorov) to a named product with some accuracy; may only describe without fully explaining the audience engagement effect.
Secure (5): sustained and accurate application of at least one named theorist (Propp or Todorov) to specific moments in a named product; explains clearly how narrative structure generates engagement (enigma, closure, character identification).
Mastering (6): sophisticated analysis using at least one theorist applied precisely to the named product; integrates enigma and closure into the argument; may compare linear and non-linear choices or consider how the structure was subverted; precise and fluent use of terminology throughout.

practice_questions.text: Which sociologist developed cultivation theory?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: C) George Gerbner. Distractors: A) Stuart Hall; B) Laura Mulvey; D) Richard Dyer.

practice_questions.text: Identify one technique of persuasive communication used in advertising.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Award for any valid technique, e.g. emotional appeal; appeal to authority; aspirational imagery; celebrity endorsement; fear appeal; creating a sense of lack without the product.

practice_questions.text: Give two differences between misrepresentation and under-representation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct points: misrepresentation = inaccurate or distorted portrayal; under-representation = absence or rarity of a group in the media; misrepresentation shows a group but in a limiting/harmful way, under-representation makes a group effectively invisible; both can send harmful messages to audiences but operate differently.

practice_questions.text: Explain what George Gerbner meant by cultivation theory and why it matters for understanding the social impact of misrepresentation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate summary of cultivation theory (heavy media consumption shapes viewers' perceptions of social reality over time); clear explanation of the consequence for misrepresented/absent groups with a developed example.
Secure: Accurate summary of the theory and at least one consequence, with a brief example.
Developing: Some understanding of the theory; may conflate cultivation theory with direct effects; consequence present but undeveloped.
Emerging: Vague reference to media having an effect on viewers; Gerbner may be named but theory is absent or wrong.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the concept of tokenism differs from genuine representation of diversity, using examples from media products you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear definition of tokenism; accurate distinction from genuine representation; two or more examples from specific products showing how tokenism manifests; analysis of why producers use tokenism and what its consequences are.
Secure: Accurate definition of tokenism; distinction from genuine diversity present; at least one example from a named product; mostly developed analysis.
Developing: Some understanding of tokenism; distinction from genuine diversity may be vague; one example present but undeveloped.
Emerging: Basic reference to representation of diversity; tokenism may be named but not accurately defined; little or no specific example.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how producer choices in a media product you have studied shape the representation of a particular social group. In your answer, consider the techniques of persuasion and audience positioning used, and evaluate how far the representation is fair or misleading.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument with a clear thesis; producer choices identified and analysed at specific moments in a named product; persuasion techniques and audience positioning both discussed; evaluation of fairness/misrepresentation is balanced and supported; at least one relevant theorist (e.g. Gerbner) applied accurately; coherent and well-structured throughout.
Secure: Clear argument; producer choices discussed with specific examples; persuasion and positioning present; evaluation of fairness attempted; some use of theory; mostly well-structured.
Developing: Some understanding of producer choices; at least two techniques discussed; evaluation of representation present but one-sided; limited use of theory.
Emerging: Basic points about how media shapes representations; answer mainly descriptive; limited specific examples; no significant use of theory.

practice_questions.text: Which term describes a person who is simultaneously a producer and a consumer of media content?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: B) Prosumer. Distractors: A) Influencer; C) Gatekeeper; D) Broadcaster.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which digital technologies have enabled self-representation by individuals and communities.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Award for any valid example, e.g. ability to publish video content on social media platforms; creating a blog or podcast; posting directly to a global audience without institutional gatekeepers; developing an audience as a social media influencer.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why the social significance of representation extends beyond what is shown in media products.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct points: representation shapes audience attitudes towards groups they may have little direct experience of; negative representation can reinforce real-world discrimination; absence from representation can limit aspiration for members of under-represented groups; news agenda-setting shapes which issues people consider important.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 'dominant representation' and why it can be difficult for contested representations to challenge it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear definition of dominant representation with specific features (repetition across many platforms, appears natural); clear explanation of why contested representations struggle (lack of institutional resources, algorithm suppression, small audiences) with at least one developed example.
Secure: Accurate definition; at least one reason for the difficulty in challenging dominant representations, with brief example.
Developing: Some understanding of dominant representation; challenge to it present but vague; limited example.
Emerging: Basic identification of some representations as powerful; limited understanding of why dominant versions persist.

practice_questions.text: Explain the concept of agenda-setting in news media and how it shapes representations of social groups, using an example from a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate definition of agenda-setting; clear explanation of how it shapes representation through selection of stories and prominence; Galtung and Ruge may be referenced accurately; specific example from a named product with detailed analysis of which groups are privileged or marginalised.
Secure: Accurate definition; representation implications present; at least one specific example with some development; theoretical reference optional but welcome.
Developing: Some understanding of agenda-setting; representation link present but undeveloped; one example present.
Emerging: Basic reference to news choosing what to cover; limited connection to representation; no specific example.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the social and political significance of representation in a media product you have studied. In your answer, consider how dominant and contested representations operate, and evaluate the impact of digital self-representation on the media landscape.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained thesis on social/political significance; dominant and contested representations both addressed with specific analysis from a named product; digital self-representation evaluated with nuance (possibilities and limits); relevant theorists (e.g. Gerbner, Galtung and Ruge) applied accurately; coherent structure throughout; counter-position considered.
Secure: Clear argument addressing significance; both representation types present; digital self-representation discussed; examples anchor the analysis; some use of theory; well-structured.
Developing: Some understanding of social significance; at least one representation type addressed; digital self-representation mentioned; limited use of theory.
Emerging: Basic points about media representation having effects; mainly descriptive; limited specific examples; little or no theory.

practice_questions.text: Which funding model requires UK households to pay a flat-rate annual charge to support a public broadcaster's content across television, radio and online services?
practice_questions.marks: The television licence fee. Distractor check: subscription = individual platform fee chosen by user; advertising revenue = commercial model; sponsorship = brand-associated funding.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which a commercial television broadcaster generates revenue other than through direct advertising.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any valid non-advertising revenue source: sponsorship (brands associated with a programme), product placement (branded products appearing within the content), direct sales of content, distribution rights sales.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain the difference between a subscription model and a freemium model.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying the distinction (subscription requires all users to pay; freemium offers a free basic tier and charges for premium access). One mark for a clear explanation with reference to how this shapes the organisation's relationship with its audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain how advertising revenue shapes the content decisions made by commercial media organisations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of how dependence on advertising revenue creates structural incentives to maximise audience size and attract advertiser-valued demographics; developed analysis of how this affects content decisions (subject matter, tone, scheduling).
Secure: Clear explanation of the link between advertising and content; some analysis of the incentives created.
Developing: Basic explanation of advertising as a funding source; link to content decisions is present but limited.
Emerging: Vague or partial description; consequences for content not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'cultural imperialism' in the context of the global media industry, using an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of cultural imperialism as the concern that globally dominant media displaces local culture and privileges specific values; well-chosen example showing how a particular media form or platform illustrates this dynamic; analytical engagement with the argument as a critical perspective rather than a simple fact.
Secure: Clear explanation of cultural imperialism; relevant example; argument about its significance made.
Developing: Some explanation; example present but underdeveloped or weakly linked.
Emerging: Basic or confused definition; example missing or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how different funding models lead to different types of media content, with reference to at least two contrasting examples from the media industries.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of how at least two contrasting funding models (e.g. public service versus commercial, subscription versus advertising) create different content priorities; specific examples used analytically to demonstrate the contrast; argument about the consequences for audiences and diversity of content; counter-position acknowledged (e.g. public broadcasters face political pressures; commercial media is not always shallow).
Secure: Clear analysis of two funding models; contrasting examples; some argument about consequences.
Developing: Some engagement with two models; examples present but analysis is mainly descriptive.
Emerging: Limited engagement with funding models; mainly one model discussed; examples absent or underdeveloped.

practice_questions.text: Which theorist developed the concept of aberrant decoding?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct answer is B. A) Incorrect — Hall developed encoding-decoding and the three reading positions. B) Correct — aberrant decoding was developed by Umberto Eco (1965). C) Incorrect — Blumler and Katz developed Uses and Gratifications. D) Incorrect — Gerbner developed cultivation theory.

practice_questions.text: Identify the reading position in which an audience accepts some aspects of the preferred meaning but modifies others.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: negotiated reading.

practice_questions.text: Identify what is meant by a 'preferred reading' and explain how a producer attempts to encode one.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for defining the preferred reading as the interpretation the producer intends the audience to accept. 1 mark for a developed explanation of how producers encode it — for example, through the selection of images, narrative framing, the values of characters positioned sympathetically, or the mode of address used by a presenter or narrator.

practice_questions.text: Explain how social variables can lead different audience members to produce different readings of the same media product.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Names one or two social variables but the explanation of their effect on reading is vague. Secure: Accurately explains how at least two social variables (e.g. age, class, gender, ethnicity) create different frames of reference that lead to different reading positions; may include a brief example. Mastering: Full, precise explanation linking specific social variables to reading positions from Hall's framework; a well-developed example showing how the same specific media product moment (e.g. a newspaper front page, a character's behaviour in a drama) could produce all three reading positions in different audience members.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the reappraisal of historical media products and why this happens.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Shows awareness that audiences read old media differently today but the explanation is superficial. Secure: Accurately explains reappraisal as the process of re-reading historical products through contemporary values, and identifies changing cultural values (e.g. on gender, race, class) as the driver. Mastering: Precise definition plus a clear account of the mechanism — original audiences decoded from within a different cultural context; contemporary audiences bring new value frameworks that make previously naturalised assumptions visible and often oppositional.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how reception theory, including Hall's reading positions and the concept of aberrant decoding, can be applied to explain how audiences respond to a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names one reading position with limited connection to a specific product. Developing: Applies two of Hall's three positions to a named product but does not clearly distinguish aberrant decoding from oppositional reading; social variables mentioned but not developed. Secure: Accurately applies all three reading positions to a named product with clear examples; correctly attributes aberrant decoding to Eco and distinguishes it from Hall's oppositional reading; identifies at least two social variables that would produce different readings. Mastering: Sustained analytical argument covering Hall's framework, Eco's aberrant decoding, and social variables; precise reference to specific moments in a named product; considers how changing cultural values could affect readings over time; structured as a coherent argument rather than a list.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the best definition of 'user-generated content'?
A. Content created by professional journalists for online platforms
B. Content edited using artificial intelligence tools
C. Media content created and published by members of the public rather than professional organisations
D. Content that has been curated by a streaming platform's algorithm
practice_questions.marks: C — Media content created and published by members of the public rather than professional organisations. Do not accept A (professional journalists), B (AI-generated), or D (algorithmically curated).

practice_questions.text: Identify one way that image manipulation technology changes the meaning of a media product.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for identifying a specific effect of image manipulation on meaning (e.g. digitally retouching a fashion advertisement creates an idealised body standard that does not reflect real human diversity, shaping audience expectations of appearance).

practice_questions.text: Identify one example of how high definition technology has changed the form or content of a media product and explain the effect it has on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a specific example of how HD has changed a media product (e.g. the close-up detail visible in prestige television drama). 1 further mark for explaining the effect on the audience (e.g. it creates a greater sense of intimacy or immediacy, or it means production design must be more detailed to maintain believability).

practice_questions.text: Explain how mobile communication technology has changed the relationship between producers and audiences in the modern media landscape.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: identifies that mobile technology allows people to create and share content (1 mark). Developing: explains how UGC has blurred the producer/consumer distinction, with one example (2 marks). Secure/Mastering: clearly explains how mobile technology has transformed production, distribution and consumption patterns, with accurate terminology (prosumer, user-generated content, digital convergence) and a specific example (3 marks).

practice_questions.text: Explain how developments in technology have changed the form or content of a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: identifies one technology with limited application to a named product (1 mark). Developing: explains how one specific technology (e.g. CGI, HD, streaming) has changed the form or content of the named product (2 marks). Secure: analyses two or more specific technological developments and their effects on the form, content or meaning of the named product, with accurate terminology (3 marks). Mastering: sophisticated analysis of how multiple technological developments have shaped the named product across production, distribution or consumption dimensions; connects technological change to audience expectation, representation or meaning (4 marks).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how developments in digital technology have changed what media products look and feel like, and how audiences consume them. Refer to a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging (1-2): identifies one or two technologies without sustained application to a named product.
Developing (3-4): explains how one or two technologies (CGI, HD, streaming, mobile, UGC) have changed the form or consumption of a named product; some accurate use of terminology.
Secure (5): sustained analysis of how multiple technological developments have shaped the named product, with clear connections between technology and the form, content or meaning of the product; accurate and consistent terminology.
Mastering (6): sophisticated analysis that integrates production, distribution and consumption dimensions; explains how technological developments have changed both what is created and how audiences experience it; considers consequences for representation, audience expectations or authenticity; precise, fluent terminology throughout.

practice_questions.text: Which theorist wrote 'Textual Poachers' (1992) and developed the concept of participatory culture?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct answer is A. A) Correct — Henry Jenkins wrote Textual Poachers and developed participatory culture theory. B) Incorrect — David Gauntlett developed identity-construction theory. C) Incorrect — Blumler and Katz developed Uses and Gratifications. D) Incorrect — Gerbner developed cultivation theory.

practice_questions.text: Identify what is meant by the term 'parasocial relationship'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a one-sided relationship in which an audience member feels familiarity or emotional connection with a media personality who does not know they exist.

practice_questions.text: Identify the difference between a person's 'actual self' and 'desired self' in Gauntlett's theory, and explain one way media use can serve each.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for accurately distinguishing actual self (current identity) from desired self (aspirational identity). 1 mark for a developed explanation of how a media product might serve each — for example, a social media user follows accounts that reflect their current interests (actual self) and accounts that represent the lifestyle they aspire to (desired self).

practice_questions.text: Explain what Jenkins means by audiences 'poaching' texts in participatory culture.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Shows awareness that fans create their own content but the connection to Jenkins is vague. Secure: Accurately explains that poaching refers to fans taking elements of existing media products and remaking or reimagining them (fan fiction, fan videos, commentary) according to their own interests, positioning audiences as active cultural participants rather than passive consumers. Mastering: Accurate explanation plus a clear account of why Jenkins saw this as culturally significant — fans are not merely consuming texts but are producing culture themselves, challenging the traditional producer-audience boundary — with a developed example context.

practice_questions.text: Explain how participatory culture and fan practices demonstrate that audiences are active rather than passive.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Notes that fans do things with media but the explanation of what makes this 'active' is limited. Secure: Explains how fan production (fan fiction, videos, commentary) constitutes active cultural participation; connects to Jenkins' concept of participatory culture and the blurring of producer-audience boundaries. Mastering: Full explanation connecting fan practices to the broader active-audience debate; contrasts with passive-audience models; notes how digital platforms have accelerated the scale of participatory culture without changing its fundamental nature (fan creativity pre-dates the internet per Jenkins).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Gauntlett's theory of identity construction and Jenkins' participatory culture theory together explain the relationship between media use and audience identity in a media form you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names one or both theorists with limited or no connection to a specific media form. Developing: Applies one theory adequately but does not connect the two theories; the link to a specific media form is surface-level. Secure: Applies both theories to a named media form with clear examples; shows how Gauntlett's identity construction and Jenkins' participatory culture are complementary rather than contradictory; uses relevant terminology (actual self, desired self, fan production, parasocial relationship). Mastering: Sustained analytical argument connecting both theories through a specific media form; explicitly links Gauntlett's identity-building function to the motivation for Jenkins' participatory production (fans produce because the text has become part of their identity); considers the social significance of these practices; structured as a coherent argument with a maintained thesis.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a 'technical code' in a moving-image media product?
A. The costume worn by a character
B. The choice of a low-angle camera shot
C. The typeface used in a headline
D. The colour of a set dressing prop
practice_questions.marks: B — The choice of a low-angle camera shot. Do not accept A (symbolic code — costume), C (verbal/print code — typography), or D (symbolic code — colour of prop).

practice_questions.text: Identify one example of intertextuality in a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for identifying a specific intertextual reference in a named media product and briefly explaining what is being referenced. The reference must be deliberate and recognisable (e.g. a music video that recreates a scene from a well-known film, or an advertisement that parodies a famous television series).

practice_questions.text: Identify one symbolic code and one technical code in a media product you have studied and explain the meaning each creates.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a symbolic code with its connotation (e.g. a character's costume connoting wealth or status). 1 further mark for identifying a technical code with its effect (e.g. a close-up shot creating intimacy or menace). Both codes must be named using accurate terminology.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by genre hybridity and why producers create hybrid genre products.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: defines genre hybridity as mixing two genres (1 mark). Developing: explains that hybrid genres combine conventions from two or more genres in a single product, with one example (2 marks). Secure/Mastering: adds that hybridity allows producers to target multiple audience communities simultaneously and gives a precise named example with the genres identified (3 marks).

practice_questions.text: Explain how conventions of a specific genre are established and communicated to audiences in a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: identifies the genre and names one convention (1 mark). Developing: identifies two or three conventions and begins to explain how they communicate genre identity to the audience (2 marks). Secure: clearly analyses how a set of genre conventions (technical, symbolic, verbal) work together in the named product to signal its genre and position audience expectations (3 marks). Mastering: sophisticated analysis applying Steve Neale's argument about repetition and difference; discusses how the product both confirms and refreshes genre conventions, with precise terminology and specific references to the named product (4 marks).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how codes and conventions are used in a media product you have studied to construct meaning and to signal its genre to an audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging (1-2): identifies one or two surface-level codes; may describe rather than analyse; limited use of genre theory.
Developing (3-4): explains how codes (at least two varieties) work together in the named product; attempts to connect codes to genre conventions; some accurate terminology.
Secure (5): sustained analysis of how technical, symbolic and/or verbal codes combine to construct specific meanings and signal genre; accurate reference to conventions and their effect on the audience; may reference Steve Neale's repetition/difference argument.
Mastering (6): sophisticated and integrated analysis of codes across multiple categories; applies genre theory (Neale) precisely; considers how conventions are confirmed or subverted and what this means for audience engagement; may discuss hybridity or intertextuality where relevant; fluent, precise terminology throughout.

before.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘analyse the codes and conventions’ of a media product, the examiner wants you to name and apply specific codes (not just say ‘the lighting is dark’ but ‘the low-key lighting, a technical code, connotes danger and moral ambiguity’). For genre questions, always name the genre, identify at least two conventions, and consider whether the product conforms to or subverts them. Mentioning Steve Neale’s argument about repetition and difference will lift a genre answer into the higher bands if the theory is actually applied to the product rather than just summarised.

practice_questions.text: Which UK regulatory body is responsible for classifying films and videos with age ratings such as U, PG, 15 and 18?
practice_questions.marks: The BBFC (British Board of Film Classification). Distractor check: OFCOM = broadcast and on-demand regulation; IPSO = press; ASA = advertising; PEGI = video games.

practice_questions.text: Identify one challenge that digital technology presents to the existing framework of media regulation in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any valid challenge: user-generated content published without pre-screening; anonymous online abuse difficult to trace; disinformation spreading faster than regulators can respond; global platforms operating across different national jurisdictions; deepfake content.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain the difference between statutory regulation and self-regulation in the media industry.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for correctly identifying the difference (statutory = legal powers granted by Parliament; self-regulatory = industry-funded voluntary system). One mark for a clear explanation of why this distinction matters, e.g. statutory bodies exercise powers set by Parliament, whereas self-regulatory bodies enforce an industry code.

practice_questions.text: Explain why some critics argue that self-regulatory bodies like IPSO cannot be fully independent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of IPSO's funding structure (industry-funded) and its voluntary membership; clear analysis of how this creates a conflict of interest; developed argument about why funding source and voluntary membership undermine genuine independence.
Secure: Accurate explanation of IPSO's structure; argument about independence limitations made; some analysis.
Developing: Basic explanation of self-regulation; independence concern noted but not well explained.
Emerging: Vague response; reasons for independence concern not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain how PEGI ratings work and why their legal enforceability in the UK since 2012 matters for the regulation of video games.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of PEGI's rating system and its age bands; clear explanation of what legal enforceability means (selling an 18-rated game to under-18s is a criminal offence); analytical engagement with why legal enforceability matters differently from advisory ratings, with reference to the contrast with other self-regulatory systems.
Secure: Accurate explanation of PEGI; legal enforceability explained; significance addressed.
Developing: Some explanation of PEGI ratings; legal enforceability noted but not well explained.
Emerging: Basic or confused account of PEGI; significance of legal enforceability not addressed.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the challenges that digital technologies present to media regulators, and evaluate whether the existing regulatory framework is adequate to address them.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of specific regulatory challenges posed by digital technologies (user-generated content, anonymous speech, global platforms, deepfakes); clear evaluation of the existing regulatory framework's strengths and limitations; reference to relevant regulatory bodies and their remits; engagement with the tension between harm prevention and freedom of expression; counter-position considered.
Secure: Clear analysis of two or more digital challenges; evaluation of regulatory adequacy; relevant regulatory bodies referenced; some engagement with the freedom/harm tension.
Developing: Some analysis of digital challenges; evaluation is limited or one-sided; regulatory bodies named but not well applied.
Emerging: Basic account of digital challenges; mainly descriptive; regulatory framework not evaluated.

practice_questions.text: In Hall's encoding-decoding model, which term describes the reading in which the audience fully accepts the preferred meaning?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: C) Dominant (preferred) reading. Distractors: A) Negotiated reading; B) Oppositional reading; D) Polysemic reading.

practice_questions.text: Identify the reading position in which an audience member partly accepts and partly challenges the preferred meaning of a media text.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Negotiated reading.

practice_questions.text: Give two social variables that can shape how an audience member decodes a media representation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct social variables: age; class; gender; ethnicity; nationality; sexuality; individual experience; religious background; political identity. Both must be listed clearly.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a negotiated and an oppositional reading of a media text, using an example from a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear and accurate definitions of both; example applied precisely to illustrate the difference between partial acceptance (negotiated) and full rejection from a different ideological position (oppositional).
Secure: Accurate definitions of both; one example present; distinction is clear if not exhaustively developed.
Developing: One position defined more clearly than the other; example present but may conflate the two positions.
Emerging: Basic attempt at one of the positions; definitions vague or confused; example absent or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Explain how social variables influence the way different audiences decode representations in a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least two social variables named and explained with precision; specific examples from a named product show how each variable would produce a different reading; encoding-decoding model referenced and accurately applied; analysis of how the same text produces different meanings in different audience segments.
Secure: At least two social variables; one named product used as example; Hall's model present and mostly accurate; two readings distinguished.
Developing: One social variable addressed; some reference to different audience responses; example present but undeveloped; Hall may be named but model not fully applied.
Emerging: Basic claim that different audiences respond differently; limited or no use of Hall; no specific product example.

practice_questions.text: Using Stuart Hall's encoding-decoding model, analyse how a media product you have studied positions its audience. In your answer, consider all three reading positions and evaluate how far the text allows for genuine audience activity in the construction of meaning.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument using Hall's model accurately; encoding discussed with reference to specific producer choices in a named product; all three reading positions applied with specific examples of how different audiences would arrive at each; polysemy and active audience concept addressed; evaluation of limits (preferred reading sets constraints) as well as freedoms; coherent thesis and structure throughout.
Secure: Hall's model accurately applied; all three readings present; specific examples from a named product; encoding and decoding both discussed; some evaluation of audience activity; well-structured.
Developing: Hall's model partially applied; at least two readings present; named product used; encoding and decoding present but analysis may be descriptive; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Basic reference to different audience responses; Hall may be named but model not accurately applied; mainly descriptive; limited specific examples.
